sections.heading: Shell mounds and burial mounds
paragraphs: The first people we can trace here lived on the terrace edge. Jōmon villagers built pit houses on the dry rim above the flooded valleys. They gathered shellfish on the mudflats below and drew water from springs at the foot of the cliff. Their shell heaps survive at Ōmori, Nakazato and Nishigahara. Nakazato is unusual. It lies on the old beach and seems to have been a place for boiling and drying shellfish.

Later local chiefs built large burial mounds shaped like keyholes. A long chain of them lines the bluff above the lower Tama River. The Noge Ōtsuka mound there was built in the 400s. Its grave goods include iron armour of the kind made in central Japan.

sections.heading: Fuchū and the province of Musashi
paragraphs: In the 600s and 700s the court in central Japan ruled through provinces. Musashi's office was at Fuchū, beside a crossing of the Tama River. Digging under and around Ōkunitama Shrine found its central layout. The office seems to have stopped working by the late 900s. A short way north stood the province's official Buddhist temple, at Kokubunji.

Musashi was a frontier province. Its dry grasslands suited horses, and the court kept horse pastures there. Families who managed land and horses became mounted warriors. Small warrior leagues and larger clans, such as the Chichibu, grew from this base.

sections.heading: Sensō-ji and Asakusa
paragraphs: Sensō-ji's founding story is set in 628. Two fishermen brothers pulled a small golden statue of Kannon from the river at Asakusa. A local leader turned his house into a shrine for it. That is the temple's own account. Historians treat the date as legend, but the temple is very old.

Asakusa stood on a sandbar beside the river now called the Sumida. Boats from the inland rivers met boats from the bay there. The temple and a river-port town grew up together. The coast road crossed the river by ferry close by. In the early 1800s the artist Aōdō Denzen engraved the temple grounds on copper, shown here.

sections.heading: The Edo family
paragraphs: In the 1100s a branch of the Chichibu clan settled on the bluff above the inlet. Edo Shigetsugu took the place name as his family name. His son, Edo Shigenaga, is better known. In 1180 he joined Minamoto no Yoritomo, who founded the Kamakura government. He helped bridge the Sumida with boats for Yoritomo's army. Their hall probably stood where the inner palace grounds are now. Under Kamakura, Edo was a small port. The family gave up the site in the 1450s and moved to Kitami, by the Tama River.

sections.heading: Ōta Dōkan's castle
paragraphs: Ōta Dōkan (1432–1486) served the Uesugi, who held this part of the Kantō. In 1457 he finished a castle at Edo. It belonged to a line of forts that faced enemies across the rivers. Kawagoe lay to the northwest; whether he also built Iwatsuki is disputed. His castle was made of earth banks and moats, not stone walls. Monks he invited wrote of ships crowding the harbour below. They brought rice, fish, salt, tea and timber from other provinces. Bigger ships anchored at Shinagawa, a few kilometres south. In 1486 his own lord had him killed.

sections.heading: The Hōjō and 1590
paragraphs: The Hōjō family of Odawara took Edo in 1524. Under them Edo became the main base for ruling Musashi. The Tōyama, a leading Hōjō family, held the castle and led its troops. In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, ruler of most of Japan, besieged Odawara. Edo castle surrendered to Tokugawa troops without a fight in the fourth month. Odawara gave up in the seventh month. Hideyoshi then moved Tokugawa Ieyasu from his home provinces to the Kantō. Ieyasu formally entered Edo on the first day of the eighth month. In today's calendar that is 30 August 1590.

sections.heading: Why Edo?
paragraphs: Why did Ieyasu settle at Edo, and not at Odawara or Kamakura? Heavy goods moved best by water. Edo sat at the head of a sheltered bay, where the rivers of the plain came down. Odawara and Kamakura faced open sea and had no river route inland. Edo also lay near the middle of Ieyasu's new lands, while Odawara lay at the far edge. The castle stood on a steep terrace edge, guarded by water. There was room to grow, with dry upland for warriors' houses and shallows to fill for a town. Edo was also far from the politics of Kyoto and Osaka. Historians still debate how much the choice was Hideyoshi's and how much Ieyasu's. From here the story moves to the Five Faces map.
